exam: A patient with sickle‑cell disease presents with new leg pain; what distinguishes vaso‑occlusive crisis pain from neuropathic pain? — Look for sudden onset, deep throbbing, no sensory loss; neuropathic pain is burning, with tingling and sensory deficits.

You suspect central sensitisation in a chronic low‑back pain patient; which bedside test helps confirm altered pain processing? — Use quantitative sensory testing (e.g., pinprick allodynia) or assess for hyperalgesia beyond the original injury site.

A malaria‑treated patient develops peripheral burning pain; which drug is the likely cause and what alternative analgesic would you choose? — Artemisinin derivatives can cause neuropathy; switch to NSAID for nociceptive component, add gabapentin if neuropathic.

In a resource‑limited hospital, a patient with suspected intra‑abdominal abscess cannot get CT; what is your next step? — Perform focused ultrasound if available; otherwise rely on clinical signs (rigid abdomen, guarding) and start broad‑spectrum antibiotics.

Why are NSAIDs contraindicated in a patient with active peptic ulcer disease presenting with pain? — NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin‑mediated gastric mucosal protection, risking perforation; use acetaminophen or opioids instead.

A HIV‑positive patient reports shooting foot pain; what investigations confirm neuropathy and what is the first‑line pharmacologic treatment? — Clinical sensory exam plus nerve conduction if possible; start amitriptyline (or gabapentin) for neuropathic pain.

During postoperative care, a patient develops uncontrolled pain despite opioids; what mechanism might be responsible and how would you address it? — Development of opioid tolerance or central sensitisation; add a NMDA antagonist (e.g., ketamine) or switch to multimodal analgesia with NSAIDs and gabapentinoids.

Explain how peripheral inflammation can lead to central sensitisation and its impact on pain thresholds. — Inflammatory mediators lower nociceptor thresholds, increase spinal cord excitability via NMDA receptors, causing amplified pain responses to normally non‑painful stimuli.
ai.title: Pain Pathways and Clinical Implications
ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Pain signals travel from peripheral receptors to the spinal cord and brain via specific neural routes. Understanding these pathways helps clinicians localise pain, recognise central sensitisation, and choose appropriate investigations and treatments, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Two main types: nociceptive (tissue injury) and neuropathic (nerve injury).
Acute pain lasts <3 months; chronic pain persists beyond tissue healing.
sections.p: Pain is an unpleasant sensory‑emotional experience that protects the body. It begins with activation of nociceptors, travels through peripheral nerves to the dorsal horn, ascends to the thalamus and cortex, and is modulated at multiple levels.

b: Gate control theory: spinal interneurons can inhibit or facilitate transmission.
Descending pathways (serotonin, norepinephrine) dampen pain; loss leads to central sensitisation.
sections.p: Peripheral nociceptors (A‑δ and C fibres) transmit signals to the dorsal horn (lamina I‑V). First‑stage visceral pain (uterine, cervical) follows sympathetic fibres to T10‑L1; second‑stage perineal pain follows pudendal (S2‑S4). Ascending tracts (spinothalamic, spinoreticular) reach the thalamus, then somatosensory cortex. The locus coeruleus releases norepinephrine, modulating pain perception.

b: COX enzymes produce prostaglandins → peripheral sensitisation.
NMDA receptor activation contributes to central sensitisation.
sections.p: Endogenous opioids (endorphins), serotonin, and norepinephrine act on spinal and supraspinal receptors to raise pain thresholds. Inflammation releases prostaglandins, lowering thresholds and enhancing transmission.

b: Peripheral neuropathy from HIV, TB drugs, or malaria treatment.
Chronic pelvic pain from untreated pelvic inflammatory disease.
Post‑surgical pain due to inadequate analgesia and infection.
sections.p: Disruption at any level can cause exaggerated or chronic pain. Central sensitisation lowers the pain threshold, causing allodynia and hyperalgesia. In low‑resource settings, infections (TB meningitis, HIV neuropathy, schistosomiasis) and herbal neurotoxins are common precipitants.

b: Visceral pain often poorly localised – consider intra‑abdominal infection.
Neuropathic pain often burning, shooting, with sensory loss.
sections.p: Accurate localisation guides diagnosis and management. Recognise red‑flag signs (e.g., unexplained weight loss, fever, neurological deficit) that suggest serious underlying disease.

t.b: Identifies pain quality, timing, aggravating/relieving factors; distinguishes nociceptive vs neuropathic pain.
Palpation, dermatomal mapping, and neurological testing localise the lesion.

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; when unavailable, rely on bedside assessment.

t.b: Is there infection or anaemia? Elevated WBC suggests bacterial infection; normal count does not exclude TB or early HIV.
Inflammatory activity? High CRP supports acute infection; ESR may be raised in chronic TB or rheumatic disease.
Is there intra‑abdominal collection or organ pathology? Detects abscess, ectopic pregnancy, schistosomal cysts.
Is neuropathy demyelinating vs axonal? Helps confirm HIV‑related neuropathy.

b: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, diclofenac) for inflammatory nociceptive pain – inhibit COX, reduce prostaglandins.
Opioids (morphine, tramadol) for severe acute pain when NSAIDs insufficient – act on µ‑receptors; avoid in respiratory compromise.
Antidepressants (amitriptyline) or anticonvulsants (gabapentin) for neuropathic pain – modulate sodium channels and NMDA activity.
Physical therapy, positioning, and local heat/cold to modulate peripheral input.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then address pain with appropriate pharmacology and non‑pharmacologic measures.

b: Acute abdomen vs. renal colic – both cause severe abdominal pain but require different imaging and surgical urgency.
Peripheral neuropathy vs. myopathy – neuropathy has sensory loss; myopathy presents with weakness without sensory change.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic pain syndromes but have different pathophysiology.

b: Normal CRP does not rule out early TB meningitis.
Ultrasound may miss small intra‑abdominal abscesses; consider repeat imaging if pain persists.
sections.p: Beware of normal labs in early infection and false‑negative imaging.

whenToSeekHelp: Unexplained new severe pain with fever, altered mental status, or neurological deficit.
Sudden loss of pain sensation (possible spinal cord compression).
Pain unresponsive to standard analgesia plus signs of sepsis.
